readAloud.text: Deep-sea mining has attracted growing interest as demand for rare metals increases. The ocean floor contains vast deposits of cobalt, nickel, and manganese, which are essential for manufacturing batteries and electronic devices. However, marine scientists warn that extracting these minerals could destroy fragile ecosystems that have taken millions of years to develop and are still poorly understood by researchers.

Studying abroad offers students far more than academic qualifications. Living in a foreign country forces young people to navigate unfamiliar customs, manage their own finances, and communicate across language barriers on a daily basis. Employers increasingly value these experiences, regarding them as evidence of adaptability, independence, and cultural awareness that cannot easily be taught in a classroom.

Fermentation is one of the oldest methods of preserving food, practised by civilisations for thousands of years. During fermentation, microorganisms such as bacteria and yeast convert sugars into acids or alcohol, which inhibit the growth of harmful microbes. Beyond preservation, the process can enhance flavour, improve digestibility, and increase the nutritional value of everyday foods.

Glass is one of the few materials that can be recycled indefinitely without any loss of quality or purity. Recycling a single glass bottle saves enough energy to power a computer for twenty-five minutes, and using recycled glass reduces both raw material consumption and furnace emissions. Despite these advantages, recycling rates vary enormously between countries, largely reflecting differences in collection systems.

Noise pollution is increasingly recognised as a serious threat to public health rather than a mere annoyance. Prolonged exposure to traffic and aircraft noise has been linked to disturbed sleep, raised blood pressure, and impaired concentration in schoolchildren. The World Health Organization now recommends that average night-time noise levels in residential areas should not exceed forty decibels.

Sports science has transformed the way elite athletes train and compete. By analysing data on heart rate, muscle activity, and movement patterns, coaches can tailor training programmes to the individual physiology of each athlete. Nutrition, recovery, and even sleep are monitored with equal precision, allowing competitors to reach peak condition while minimising the risk of injury.

Museums are embracing digital technology to attract younger audiences and bring their collections to life. Interactive touchscreens, augmented reality headsets, and three-dimensional reconstructions allow visitors to examine fragile artefacts in ways that were previously impossible. Some institutions have also digitised their entire archives, making millions of objects freely accessible to researchers and the public around the world.

retellLecture.title: Crowdsourcing in scientific research
retellLecture.sample: The lecture explained how crowdsourcing is used in scientific research. The speaker described citizen science projects in which volunteers classify galaxies or transcribe historical weather records, tasks computers still do poorly. The main advantages are speed and low cost, allowing researchers to analyse enormous datasets. However, the speaker noted concerns about data quality, which projects address by having several volunteers check the same item.
retellLecture.text: In recent years, scientists have increasingly turned to crowdsourcing, asking ordinary members of the public to help process research data. One famous project invites volunteers to classify the shapes of galaxies from telescope images, a task at which human eyes still outperform computers. Another asks people to transcribe handwritten weather logs from nineteenth-century ships, turning them into digital records that help climate researchers model long-term change. The advantages are clear: tasks that would take a small research team decades can be completed by thousands of volunteers in weeks, at almost no cost. Naturally, there are concerns about accuracy, since volunteers are not trained scientists. Projects therefore build in safeguards, typically showing each image or record to several different people and accepting only classifications where they agree. When designed carefully, crowdsourced science has proven remarkably reliable, and it also gives the public a genuine stake in discovery.

retellLecture.title: Wildfires: destruction and renewal
retellLecture.sample: The lecture discussed wildfires, explaining that although they cause enormous destruction, they are also a natural and necessary part of many ecosystems. Some plants, such as certain pine trees, actually need fire to release their seeds. The speaker warned that climate change and decades of suppressing all fires have made modern wildfires larger and more dangerous, and suggested controlled burning as a management strategy.
retellLecture.text: Wildfires are usually reported as pure disasters, destroying homes, forests, and wildlife habitats, and releasing huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Yet fire has always been a natural part of many ecosystems, and some species depend on it. Certain pine trees, for example, produce cones that only open and release their seeds when exposed to intense heat, and fires clear away dead undergrowth, returning nutrients to the soil and letting sunlight reach young plants. The problem is that modern wildfires are becoming unnaturally severe. Climate change brings hotter, drier summers, while decades of extinguishing every small fire have allowed dense fuel to accumulate in forests. As a result, when fires do start, they burn with exceptional intensity. Many land managers now carry out controlled burns in cool seasons, deliberately reducing fuel so that inevitable future fires remain smaller, cooler, and less destructive.

respondToSituation.prompt: You are working on a group presentation worth 40 percent of your course grade. One member of your group has missed every meeting and has not done any of their assigned work. The presentation is in five days. Speak to this group member. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You are working on a group presentation worth 40 percent of your course grade. One member of your group has missed every meeting and has not done any of their assigned work. The presentation is in five days. Speak to this group member. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hi, thanks for meeting me. I wanted to talk about the group presentation, because honestly we're all getting quite worried. You've missed the last three meetings, and the section you agreed to research still hasn't been started. This project is worth forty percent of our grade, so it affects all of us. Is everything okay? If you're struggling with the workload or something else is going on, please tell us — maybe we can rearrange the tasks. But if you can't contribute, we need to know now so we can divide your part between us, and we might have to mention the situation to our tutor. We'd really rather sort this out together as a team. So what do you think — can you take on a smaller section and have it ready by Wednesday?

respondToSituation.prompt: You bought a ticket for a concert, but on the day of the event you fell ill and could not attend. The ticket was expensive. Email the ticket company to ask about a refund or exchange. What would you write/say?
respondToSituation.audio: You bought a ticket for a concert, but on the day of the event you fell ill and could not attend. The ticket was expensive. Email the ticket company to ask about a refund or exchange. What would you write/say?
respondToSituation.sample: Dear customer service team, I am writing regarding my ticket for last Saturday's concert, order number TK-8834. Unfortunately, I fell ill on the day of the event and was unable to attend; I have attached a doctor's note as confirmation. I completely understand that tickets are normally non-refundable, but as the ticket was quite expensive, I would like to ask whether any exception is possible. Ideally, I would appreciate a refund, but I would gladly accept an exchange for a future event or credit towards another booking instead. I have been a loyal customer for several years and have never requested anything like this before. Please let me know what options are available. Thank you very much for your understanding, and I look forward to your reply. Kind regards, Alex.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should all university students be required to spend a semester studying abroad?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students discussed whether a semester abroad should be compulsory. Speaker A strongly supported the idea, saying it builds independence and language skills that employers value. Speaker B objected that compulsory schemes are unfair to students who cannot afford extra costs or who have family responsibilities, and suggested generous scholarships instead. Speaker C proposed a middle ground: making study abroad optional but actively encouraged, with short-term programmes for those unable to go for a full semester. They agreed the experience was valuable but disagreed about making it mandatory.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I think it should absolutely be compulsory. Spending a semester in another country completely changes you — you become independent, you pick up another language, and employers genuinely look for that kind of experience on a CV. If it's optional, most people never bother, and they miss out.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That sounds great if your parents can pay for it. Flights, visas, higher rent in some cities — plenty of students simply can't afford that, and some have part-time jobs or family members they care for. Making it mandatory punishes the students who are already struggling. I'm fine with encouraging it, but requiring it is unfair.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But universities could provide funding. If everyone went, the scheme would be huge, and costs could be negotiated down.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Maybe the answer is flexibility. Keep it optional, but actively promote it with proper scholarships, and offer shorter alternatives — say, a four-week summer programme — for students who genuinely can't commit to a whole semester. That way almost everyone gets some international experience without forcing anyone into debt.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I could support that. Short programmes plus real financial help would solve most of my objections.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'd still prefer it to be the default option rather than something students have to opt into, but I'd accept that as a compromise.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Drone delivery services in cities: benefit or nuisance?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The group debated drone delivery in cities. Speaker A welcomed it, highlighting faster deliveries, lower emissions than vans, and reduced road congestion. Speaker B raised serious concerns about noise, safety failures, and privacy, arguing that regulation should come before expansion. Speaker C took a balanced view, supporting drones for urgent medical deliveries but questioning their use for routine shopping. Overall, the group agreed drones have real potential but need strict rules on routes, altitude and operating hours.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I'm really excited about drone delivery. Parcels arrive in thirty minutes, delivery vans come off the roads, and the drones are electric, so emissions drop. For urgent things like medicine it could literally save lives.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Or it could be a nightmare. Imagine hundreds of buzzing drones over your garden all day. What happens when one malfunctions and falls onto a busy street? And they'll all have cameras filming everything below them. We need strict regulation before these services expand, not after.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: I think both of you have a point. For medical emergencies — delivering defibrillators or blood supplies — drones are clearly brilliant. But do we really need drones bringing people takeaway coffee? The benefit there is tiny compared with the noise.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Fair enough, but the technology gets better and quieter the more it's used. If we restrict it too much, companies will just test elsewhere.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Then let's allow it with conditions: fixed flight corridors away from homes, no flying at night, and a proper licensing system.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: That seems like a sensible way forward — encourage the valuable uses while protecting residents from the downsides.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Microplastics, fragments of plastic smaller than five millimetres, have been detected throughout the food chain, from seafood and salt to drinking water and even fruit and vegetables. Scientists have confirmed that humans consume tens of thousands of these particles every year, yet the consequences for health remain uncertain. Laboratory experiments show that high concentrations of microplastics can cause inflammation and cell damage in animals, but the doses used in such studies far exceed what people typically ingest. Complicating matters further, plastic particles can carry toxic chemicals and harmful bacteria on their surfaces, potentially transporting them into the body. Researchers agree that the greatest difficulty is measurement: there is no standardised method for detecting the smallest particles in human tissue, so estimates of exposure vary widely. Until long-term studies are completed, most experts advise a precautionary approach, urging consumers and policymakers to reduce plastic waste even though the precise risks are not yet fully understood.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Although humans ingest tens of thousands of microplastic particles annually through food and water, the health effects remain unclear because laboratory studies use unrealistically high doses and no standardised measurement method exists, so experts recommend reducing plastic waste as a precaution while long-term research continues.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Machine translation has improved beyond recognition in little more than a decade. Earlier systems translated word by word according to grammatical rules, producing output that was often comically inaccurate. Modern systems, by contrast, use neural networks trained on millions of human-translated texts, allowing them to capture context, idiom, and tone with remarkable success. For routine tasks such as translating product manuals or news summaries, machines now rival professional human translators in both speed and adequacy, at a fraction of the cost. Nevertheless, significant weaknesses remain. Literary translation still demands human creativity, since machines struggle with wordplay, cultural allusion, and deliberate ambiguity. Moreover, because neural systems learn from existing translations, they can reproduce and even amplify the biases contained in those texts. Most industry observers therefore predict not the disappearance of human translators but a transformation of their role: professionals increasingly edit and certify machine output rather than translating from scratch.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Neural machine translation, trained on millions of human translations, now matches professional quality for routine texts at far lower cost, but because it still fails at literary creativity and inherits biases from its training data, human translators are expected to shift toward editing and certifying machine output rather than disappearing.

essay.prompt: Some people believe that international tourism damages local cultures and environments, while others argue it brings essential economic benefits. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.
essay.sample: Possible structure: (1) Introduction — paraphrase the debate, state your position. (2) Arguments against tourism: overcrowding of historic sites, pollution and pressure on water supplies, traditions turned into commercial performances, rising prices driving out local residents. (3) Arguments for tourism: major source of employment and foreign currency, funds conservation of monuments and national parks, encourages infrastructure that locals also use, promotes cross-cultural understanding. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. tourism is beneficial overall but must be managed sustainably through visitor limits and local investment. Useful phrases: 'It is frequently claimed that…', 'Critics point out that…', 'A strong counter-argument is…', 'On balance, I am convinced that…'

summarizeSpokenText.title: The debate over deep-sea mining
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture examined the debate over deep-sea mining. Supporters argue that mining the ocean floor could supply the metals needed for batteries and reduce the environmental and ethical problems of land mining. Opponents warn that deep-sea ecosystems are largely unknown and that mining could cause irreversible damage, including sediment plumes that smother marine life. The speaker concluded that many scientists are calling for a pause until more research is done.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: The demand for metals like cobalt and nickel, essential for electric vehicle batteries, has turned attention to the deepest parts of the ocean, where potato-sized nodules rich in these metals lie scattered across the seabed. Supporters of deep-sea mining argue that collecting these nodules could supply the green energy revolution while avoiding the deforestation, pollution, and child labour associated with some mines on land. The nodules, they point out, simply sit on the surface, so no digging or blasting is required. Opponents respond that we know astonishingly little about deep-sea life. The regions targeted for mining may contain millions of species never yet described by science, and the sediment clouds raised by mining machines could drift for kilometres, smothering organisms far from the actual site. Because these ecosystems grow and recover extremely slowly, damage could persist for thousands of years. Many marine scientists are therefore calling for a moratorium until far more research has been completed.

summarizeSpokenText.title: How wildfires have become megafires
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture explained why wildfires have grown into destructive megafires. Fire is natural and many ecosystems need it, but two factors have made fires worse: climate change producing hotter, drier conditions, and a century of suppressing all fires, which let fuel build up. The speaker described how megafires create their own weather, and recommended controlled burning and better land management to reduce the danger.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: In the past few decades, wildfires in many regions have grown so large and intense that a new word was invented for them: megafires. Fire itself is nothing new — forests and grasslands have burned for millions of years, and many species actually depend on regular burning. Two human factors, however, have changed the equation. The first is climate change: hotter temperatures and longer droughts dry out vegetation, turning forests into tinder. The second is a century of well-intentioned but misguided policy. For generations, fire services extinguished every blaze as quickly as possible. Without small, frequent fires to clear it away, dead wood accumulated year after year, so when fire finally escapes control, it burns with terrifying intensity. The largest megafires generate so much heat that they create their own weather systems, including fire tornadoes and lightning that ignites new blazes. Experts increasingly recommend a return to controlled burning, deliberately setting small fires in safe conditions to reduce the fuel waiting for the next big one.

Yet recycling rates differ dramatically between countries, and the reasons are mainly practical rather than cultural. Nations with deposit-return schemes, where consumers pay a small deposit refunded when they return the bottle, consistently achieve rates above ninety percent.
